html:
The fur trade was the buying and selling of animal pelts, above all from the cold forests of Siberia and northern North America. From the 1500s to the 1800s it drove explorers, traders and empires deep into the north.

In Russia, furs, especially sable, were the treasure that pulled Cossacks and traders east across Siberia in the 1600s; see the Russian conquest of Siberia. They forced the peoples of Siberia to pay a fur tribute called yasak.

In North America the prize was beaver, whose felted fur made the best hats in Europe:

  • New France lived on it. French traders and their Huron, Algonquin and Odawa partners carried furs to Montreal and Quebec.
  • The Dutch built New Amsterdam partly to guard a fur trade up the Hudson River with the Mohawk and Mahican.
  • From 1670 the Hudson's Bay Company traded from posts on Hudson Bay, and its rival the North West Company pushed across the continent.
  • After 1778 a sea otter trade linked the Nuu-chah-nulth coast to China.

For Native peoples the trade brought metal tools, guns, cloth and blankets, but also dependence, disease and wars over hunting grounds, like the Beaver Wars of the 1600s. The hunting peoples of the subarctic shifted their lives toward trapping. By the mid-1800s beaver had been overhunted, hat fashions changed to silk, and the trade faded.
